rows.speaker: عاصم ويعقوب
rows.claim: Asim and Yaqub read with third-person yāʾ; Ibn ʿĀshūr says this clarifies that the majority reading addresses the polytheists.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عاصم ويعقوب { يدعون } بالتحتية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Resurrection follows divine oneness because both principles invalidate polytheism; this prepares the link between denying resurrection and denying oneness.
rows.anchor: لأن هذين هما أصل إبطال عقيدة المشركين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronouns in “they perceive” and “they are raised” refer to unbelievers: by iltifāt in the majority reading and by pronoun consistency in Asim and Yaqub’s reading.
rows.anchor: عائدان إلى الكفار على طريق الالتفات في قراءة الجمهور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their ignorance of the resurrection’s timing threatens them: the resurrection they deny will happen, and they do not know when it will overtake them.
rows.anchor: والمقصود من نفي شعورهم بالبعث تهديدهم بأن البعث الذي أنكروه واقع وأنهم لا يدرون متى يبغتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Baʿth literally means sending from one place to another and also stirring something settled, as when a camel is roused; the latter may name the cause for its result.
rows.anchor: والبعث : حقيقته الإرسال من مكان إلى آخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Qurʾānic usage, baʿth is bringing people to judgment after death: the dead rise from graves, while those alive at the world's end are raised by revival after their death.
rows.anchor: وقد غلب البعث في اصطلاح القرآن على إحضار الناس إلى الحساب بعد الموت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “they do not perceive” cannot refer to the idols invoked, since idols are not the ones threatened with resurrection.
rows.anchor: ولا يستقيم أن يكون ضمير يشعرون } عائدا إلى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ayyān is an interrogative of time formed from ayy and ān (“which time”); the question suspends yashʿurūn, meaning they sense no time for their raising.
rows.anchor: مركبة من ( أي ) و ( آن ) بمعنى أي زمن

none: The segment only quotes the verses and supplies a bare heading.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The small price is what the polytheists promised converts—money and comfortable living—if they abandoned Islam.
rows.anchor: الثمن القليل هو ما يعدهم به المشركون إن رجعوا عن الإسلام من مال وهناء عيش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prohibition bars breaking Islam’s covenant to recover benefits forfeited by entering Islam; it connects with warnings against breaking oaths and using them deceitfully, each addressing a motive for breach.
rows.anchor: وهذا نهي عن نقض عهد الإسلام لأجل ما فاتهم بدخولهم في الإسلام من منافع عند قوم الشرك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thaman is compensation received in an exchange; qaleelan is explanatory, not restrictive, since every price for breaking God’s covenant is little, however great the gain.
rows.anchor: والثمن : العوض الذي يأخذه المعاوض .

words: إِنَّمَا عِندَ ٱللَّهِ هُوَ خَيْرٌ لَّكُمْ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement that what is with God is better explains the prohibition: God’s recompense surpasses every exchange, however large.
rows.anchor: وجملة { إنما عند الله هو خير لكم } تعليل للنهي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: What God has stored for Muslims includes good in this life and the next; the promised worldly good exceeds the polytheists’ offer, and the afterlife’s good exceeds all else.
rows.anchor: و ( ما عند الله ) هو ما ادخره للمسلمين من خير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here “with God” means kept in store for believers, unlike verses where “with Him” describes God’s possession of the unseen or His treasuries.
rows.anchor: وليست عندية ملك الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Innamā combines inna with relative mā, not the particle that renders inna non-operative; it should be written apart, though the muṣḥaf joins it by pronunciation, inconsistently elsewhere.
rows.anchor: فحقها أن تكتب مفصولة ( ما ) عن ( إن )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “If you know” means knowing the true consequences of things and not being deceived by immediate gain; it urges reflection and understanding.
rows.anchor: ومعنى { إن كنتم تعلمون } إن كنتم تعلمون حقيقة عواقب الأشياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The contrast between what people possess and what God has is a concluding restatement explaining why God’s promised good is better: His gift endures while human gifts run out.
rows.anchor: وجملة { ما عندكم ينفد وما عند الله باق } تذييل وتعليل لمضمون جملة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nafād means depletion or extinction; baqāʾ means not ceasing to exist.
rows.anchor: والنفاد : الانقراض . والبقاء : عدم الفناء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since God’s provision does not perish, believers should rely on His promised gift for Islam rather than human gifts, however plentiful.
rows.anchor: أي ما عند الله لا يفنى فالأجدر الاعتماد على عطاء الله الموعود على الإسلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The line is generalized like a proverb; “what you have” addresses all people and covers what both promisers and promise-recipients possess, though the warned believers hold nothing.
rows.anchor: وبقرينة المقابلة بما عند لله ، أي ما عندكم أيها الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because obedience means forgoing the polytheists’ immediate offer, God promises reward to those who endure patiently.
rows.anchor: ولما كان في نهيهم عن أخذ ما يعدهم به المشركون حمل لهم على حرمانن أنفسهم

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read with third-person yāʾ, referring to God as the one who forbids, promises, and rewards obedience.
rows.anchor: قرأه الجمهور وليجزين } بياء الغيبة

rows.speaker: ابن كثير وعاصم وابن ذكوان عن ابن عمر وأبو جعفر
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir, Asim, Ibn Dhakwan (in one narration from Ibn ʿUmar), and Abu Jaʿfar read with the first-person plural of majesty, an iltifāt.
rows.anchor: وقرأه ابن كثير وعاصم وابن ذكوان عن ابن عمر في إحدى روايتين عنه وأبو جعفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ajrahum is the second object of yujziyan, construed with the two-object verb meaning “to give.”
rows.anchor: و { أجرهم } منصوب على المفعولية الثانية ل ( يجزين )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bāʾ marks cause, and aḥsan is an intensive superlative: the reward is for the especially good deed of remaining Muslim while enduring persecution.
rows.anchor: والباء للسببية . و ( أحسن ) صيغة تفضيل مستعملة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise is emphatic, marked by the oath lām and emphatic nūn.
rows.anchor: وقد أكد الوعد بلام القسم ونون التوكيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 97 generalizes the prior promise to everyone matching the warned group in steadfastness and righteous action, and clarifies the reward; both functions set it apart as a new sentence.
rows.anchor: لما كان الوعد المتقدم بقوله تعالى ؛ { وليجزين الذين صبروا أجرهم بأحسن ما كانوا يعملون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase explains the general scope of the relative pronoun man and shows that Islamic rulings apply equally to men and women except where the religion specifies otherwise.
rows.anchor: تبيين للعموم الذي دلت عليه { من } الموصولة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise first says God will give life so it can specify the kind of life; the life itself is foregrounded, with divine attribution honoring its recipient.
rows.anchor: وذكر ( لنحيينه ) ليبنى عليه بيان نوع الحياة بقوله تعالى : { حياة طيبة }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Life’s fixed duration stands for the quality of what occurs during it, so “good life” is a rational metaphor for good experiences; believers who die are compensated for the promised good they missed.
rows.anchor: فوصفها بالطيب بهذا الاعتبار ، أي طيب ما يحصل فيها ، فهذا الوصف مجاز عقلي

rows.speaker: خباب بن الأرت
rows.claim: In a report in the Ṣaḥīḥ, Khabbāb says the emigrants sought God’s pleasure and their reward was assured: Muṣʿab died at Uḥud with only a short shroud, while others later enjoyed its fruits.
rows.anchor: ويفسر هذا المعنى ما ورد في الصحيح عن خباب بن الأرت قال : ( هاجرنا مع رسول الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭayyib means pleasant or good, opposite to foul and bad.
rows.anchor: والطيب : ما يطيب ويحسن . وضد الطيب : الخبيث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise concerns worldly blessings, especially contentment with one’s allotment, hopeful expectation, health, well-being, and the dignity of Islam in believers’ hearts; these differ with inner states and aspirations.
rows.anchor: وهذا وعد بخيرات الدنيا . وأعظمها الرضى بما قسم لهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This sentence follows the statement of God’s dominion in 20:6, adding the breadth of His knowledge; it precedes 20:8, while its original order would place the conditional clause after the assertion.
rows.anchor: عطف على جملة { له ما في السموات وما في الأرض } ( طه : 6 ) لدلالة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conditional phrase is parenthetical between “He knows the secret and what is more hidden” and “God—there is no deity but Him”; presenting the assertion as proof of its actuality is madhhab kalāmī.
rows.anchor: وأصل النظم : ويعلم السر وأخفى إن تجهر بالقول ؛ فموقع قوله : { وإن تجهر بالقول }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God knows the secret and what is still more hidden even when someone speaks aloud to be heard; loudness adds nothing because He already knows the secret.
rows.anchor: والمعنى : إنه يعلم السر وأخفى من السر في الأحوال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A conditional form can assert what holds in every case rather than make the result contingent; the cited examples use it to express universality.
rows.anchor: وذلك في كل شرط لا يقصد به التعليق بل يقصد التحقيق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Kabīr’s “when the anxious one sleeps” illustrates a condition meaning that the subject stays wakeful whenever others sleep.
rows.anchor: سهدا إذا ما نام ليل الهوجل

rows.speaker: بشامة بن حزن النهشلي
rows.claim: Bashāma’s conditional about warriors drawing back exemplifies a condition used to assert what happens whenever the circumstance occurs.
rows.anchor:
وقول بشامة بن حزن النهشلي :
إذا الكماة تنحوا أن يصيبهم
حد الظبات وصلناها بأيدينا

rows.speaker: إبراهيم بن كنيف النبهاني
rows.claim: Ibrāhīm’s conditional about the days’ reversals presents steadfastness as holding through every turn of fortune.
rows.anchor:
وقول إبراهيم بن كنيف النبهاني :
فإن تكن الأيام جالت صروفها
ببؤسى ونعمى والحوادث تفعل

rows.speaker: القطامي
rows.claim: Al-Quṭāmī’s question about whether civilization impresses someone is another conditional used rhetorically to generalize.
rows.anchor:
وقول القطامي :
فمن تكن الحضارة أعجبته
فأي رجال بادية ترانا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address may be to the Prophet, with others included, or to no particular person, in which case it addresses everyone.
rows.anchor: فالخطاب في قوله وإن تجهر } يجوز أن يكون خطابا للنبيء صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse singles out what is heard because secret speech is ordinarily among the hardest things for people to know.
rows.anchor: واختير في إثبات سعة علم الله تعالى خصوص علمه بالمسموعات لأن السر أخفى الأشياء عن علم الناس

rows.speaker: عبدالله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Al-Bukhārī reports from Ibn Masʿūd that three men near the Kaʿba debated whether God hears quiet speech; one concluded that if He hears them aloud, He also hears them secretly.
rows.anchor: وفي ( صحيح البخاري ) عن عبدالله بن مسعود قال : اجتمع عند البيت ثقفيان وقرشي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr thinks this verse alludes to the same dispute recalled in 41:22, and links it to God knowing what people conceal beneath their clothes.
rows.anchor: ولا أحسب هذه الآية إلا ناظرة إلى مثل ما نظرت الآية الآنفة الذكر .

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although secret speech might seem more apt to demonstrate divine omniscience, the choice to posit loud speech suits this context and the Ibn Masʿūd report.
rows.anchor: يبقى النظر في توجيه الإتيان بهذا الشرط بطريقة الاعتراض ، وتوجيه اختيار فرض الشرط بحالة الجهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr proposes that the condition concerns the Prophet’s effort to recite aloud; as with 7:205, it may have been superseded by 15:94, teaching equal divine knowledge of open and quiet supplication and rejecting the polytheists’ assumption.
rows.anchor: وأحسب لفرض الشرط بحالة الجهر بالقول خصوصية بهذا السياق اقتضاها اجتهاد النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qawl is a verbal noun for a person’s utterance and includes recitation, supplication, and conversation; here recitation is especially relevant to the following verses.
rows.anchor: والقول : مصدر ، وهو تلفظ الإنسان بالكلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conditional apodosis is omitted and supplied by “He knows the secret and what is more hidden”: do not strain yourself, since loud speech has no advantage.
rows.anchor: وجواب شرط { وإن تجهر بالقول } محذوف يدل عليه قوله : { فإنه يعلم السر وأخفى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse’s main point is not how people should supplicate: the Sunna establishes loud supplication and remembrance, so that issue is relevant here only by implication.
rows.anchor: وبهذا تعلم أن ليس مساق الآية لتعليم الناس كيفية الدعاء ، فقد ثبت في السنة الجهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Akhfā is a comparative with its comparison elided: “more hidden than the secret”; it refers to inner speech and sounds quieter than whispered speech.
rows.anchor: وأخفى اسم تفضيل ، وحذف المفضل عليه لدلالة المقام عليه ، أي وأخفى من السر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The declaration that God alone is deity and owns the best names concludes the preceding discussion, gathering the divine actions, creation, and majesty already described.
rows.anchor: تذييل لما قبله لأن ما قبله تضمن صفات من فعل الله تعالى ومن خلقه ومن عظمته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Allah” is the predicate of an omitted subject: the construction means “He is God,” as in the earlier discussion of 20:5.
rows.anchor: واسم الجلالة خبر لمبتدأ محذوف . والتقدير : هو الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both “there is no deity but Him” and “to Him belong the best names” are circumstantial clauses attached to Allah.
rows.anchor: وجملة { لا إلاه إلا هو } حال من اسم الجلالة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Names are words denoting possession of real attributes; for God they are the unique proper name Allah or descriptive names such as al-Raḥmān and al-Jabbār.
rows.anchor: والأسماء : الكلمات الدالة على الاتصاف بحقائق . وهي بالنسبة إلى الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fronting “to Him” restricts the best names to God: idols have empty names, human qualities fall short of divine perfection, and human claims to pride are false.
rows.anchor: وتقديم المجرور في قوله { له الأسماء الحسنى } للاختصاص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The names are best because they signify perfect realities in God; even Allah, a proper name, began as a description of exclusive divinity, necessary existence, and deserved worship.
rows.anchor: ووصف الأسماء بالحسنى لأنها دالة على حقائق كاملة بالنسبة إلى المسمى بها تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr points to the earlier command to God’s names in 7:180.
rows.anchor: وقد تقدم شيء من هذا عند قوله تعالى : { ولله الأسماء الحسنى فادعوه بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Moses story follows reassurance about conveying the Qurʾān, modeling patience under prophetic burdens and consoling the Prophet that deniers share earlier rejecters’ fate; later passages return to that warning and to patience after Adam’s story.
rows.anchor: أعقب تثبيت الرسول على التبليغ والتنويه بشأن القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Has the story reached you?” is coordinated with 20:2 to suit the preceding discourse; parts of Moses’ story appeared in al-Aʿrāf and Yūnus.
rows.anchor: فجملة { وهل أتاك حديث موسى } عطف على جملة { ما أنزلنا عليك القرآن لتشقى }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question is a figurative invitation to anticipation, whether this is the first telling to the Prophet or not; “when he saw a fire” heightens suspense.
rows.anchor: والاستفهام مستعمل في التشويق إلى الخبر مجازا وليس مستعملا في حقيقته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hal is chosen for its sense of confirmation, as qad does in a declarative sentence.
rows.anchor: وأوثر حرف ( هل ) في هذا المقام لما فيه من معنى التحقيق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥadīth means a report recounting an event that occurred; its plural aḥādīth is irregular, and al-Farrāʾ says its singular was first aḥdūtha.
rows.anchor: والحديث : الخبر ، وهو اسم للكلام الذي يحكى به أمر حدث في الخارج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Idh is an adverb attached to the story; the sight of fire allows many scenarios and heightens suspense.
rows.anchor: وإذ } ظرف للحديث . وقد تقدم نظائره ، وخص هذا الظرف بالذكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seeing fire indicates night and that Moses needed fire, explaining his instruction to his family to wait.
rows.anchor: ورؤية النار تدل على أن ذلك كان بليل ، وأنه كان بحاجة إلى النار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ahl means his wife and children; the plural command confirms they were with him, and Exodus also says Moses traveled with wife and sons on donkeys toward Egypt.
rows.anchor: والأهل : الزوج والأولاد . وكانوا معه بقرينة الجمع في قوله { امكثوا

rows.speaker: حمزة وخلف
rows.claim: The majority read the hāʾ in ahlihi with kasra; Ḥamza and Khalaf read it with ḍamma, assimilating to the following hamzat al-waṣl.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور بكسر هاء ضمير أهله على الأصل . وقرأه حمزة وخلف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Īnās is seeing clearly, without uncertainty.
rows.anchor: والإيناس : الإبصار البين الذي لا شبهة فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The emphatic inna signals the importance of good news to his family in darkness.
rows.anchor: وتأكيد الخبر بإن لقصد الاهتمام به بشارة لأهله إذ كانوا في الظلمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qabas is a flame or ember taken from a burning source, such as a coal or firebrand; this implies darkness and no means to kindle fire.
rows.anchor: والقبس : ما يؤخذ اشتعاله من اشتعال شيء ويقبس ، كالجمرة من مجموع الجمر

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: An alternative says Moses tried to strike a spark with his flint, but it failed to catch.
rows.anchor: وقيل : اقتدح زنده فصلد ، أي لم يقدح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Finding guidance by the fire means finding someone who knows the route and is traveling in the same direction, so he can guide Moses.
rows.anchor: ومعنى أو أجد على النار هدى } : أو ألقى عارفا بالطريق قاصدا السير فيما أسير فيه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One explanation says Moses had lost the road in intense darkness and wanted to travel by night.
rows.anchor: قيل : كان موسى قد خفي عليه الطريق من شدة الظلمة وكان يحب أن يسير ليلا .

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aw expresses a choice: taking a flame is certain, while he might also find and accompany someone who knows the route.
rows.anchor: و { أو } هنا للتخيير ، لأن إتيانه بقبس أمر محقق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAlā is figuratively spatial: it means very near the fire, as someone tends it for light or warmth; al-Aʿshā’s verse uses the same sense.
rows.anchor: وحرف { على } في قوله : { أو أجد على النار هدى } مستعمل في الاستعلاء المجازي

rows.speaker: الأعشى
rows.claim: Al-Aʿshā uses ʿalā with the sense of being close to the fire.
rows.anchor:
قال الأعشى :
وبات على النار الندى والمحلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God inspired Moses to say hudā, anticipating that he would find great guidance at the fire and bring his people benefit.
rows.anchor: وقد أجرى الله على لسان موسى معنى هذه الكلمة إلهاما إياه أنه سيجد عند تلك النار هدى عظيما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fire is a subtle divine symbol: seeking light in darkness foreshadows revelation illuminating people with true religion after misguidance and false belief.
rows.anchor: وإظهار النار لموسى رمز رباني لطيف ؛ إذ جعل اجتلابه لتلقي الوحي باستدعاء بنور في ظلمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passive “he was called” heightens anticipation by withholding the caller’s identity; “I am your Lord” then reveals it and depicts the unknown voice Moses heard.
rows.anchor: بني فعل النداء للمجهول زيادة في التشويق إلى استطلاع القصة ، فإبهام المنادي يشوق سامع الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses recognized a divine address because unusual created sounds came from no visible person or angelic intermediary; they signified God’s intent, the inner speech subsisting in God beyond letters, sounds, or hearing.
rows.anchor: والمراد التي تدل عليه تلك الأصوات الخارقة للعادة هو ما نسميه بالكلام النفسي . وليس الكلام النفسي هو الذي سمعه موسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling himself Moses’ Lord calms his fear of an unseen speaker, since a lord is gentle toward the one under his care.
rows.anchor: والإخبار عن ضمير المتكلم بأنه رب المخاطب لتسكين روعة نفسه من خطاب لا يرى مخاطبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Inna confirms the surprising message and prevents Moses from doubting the source of the speech.
rows.anchor: وتأكيد الخبر بحرف ( إن ) لتحقيقه لأجل غرابته دفعا لتطرق الشك عن موسى في مصدر هذا الكلام

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو وابن كثير
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr and Ibn Kathīr read annī with fatḥa on the hamza, taking an omitted preposition: “he was called that I am your Lord”; emphasis remains in either reading.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عمرو وابن كثير ( أني ) بفتح الهمزة على حذف باء الجر . والتقدير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to remove the sandals follows the declaration of lordship to signal that the place became sacred through divine speech occurring there.
rows.anchor: وتفريع الأمر بخلع النعلين على الإعلام بأنه ربه إشارة إلى أن ذلك المكان قد حله التقديس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khalaʿ means separating something attached; sandals are thick leather foot coverings tied with leather straps to protect against ground and stones.
rows.anchor: والخلع : فصل شيء عن شيء كان متصلا به . والنعلان : جلدان غليظان يجعلان تحت الرجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God ordered Moses to remove his sandals to honor the place where he would hear divine speech.
rows.anchor: وإنما أمره الله بخلع نعليه تعظيما منه لذلك المكان الذي سيسمع فيه الكلام الإلهي

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Al-Tirmidhī transmits from Ibn Masʿūd, from the Prophet, that Moses’ sandals were made of the hide of a dead donkey.
rows.anchor: وروى الترمذي عن ابن مسعود عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال : ( كانت نعلاه من جلد حمار ميت )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command also conveys humility, but this circumstance does not establish a general requirement to remove sandals during prayer.
rows.anchor: أقول : وفيه أيضا زيادة خشوع . وقد اقتضى كلا المعنيين قوله تعالى : { إنك بالواد المقدس }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wād is a pass between mountains or hills, originally ending in yāʾ; the yāʾ is often dropped but retained in the dual and annexation.
rows.anchor: والواد : المفرج بين الجبال والتلالل . وأصله بياء في آخره .

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muqaddas means purified and sanctified; places become sacred through honored events occurring there, here the divine address.
rows.anchor: والمقدس : المطهر المنزه . وتقدم في قوله تعالى : { ونقدس لك في أول البقرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭuwā has been read with either ḍamma or kasra, though the well-known reading has only ḍamma.
rows.anchor: وهو بضم الطاء وبكسرها ، ولم يقرأ في المشهور إلا بضم الطاء

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One view takes Ṭuwā as the proper name of the valley.
rows.anchor: فقيل : اسم لذلك المكان

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view treats Ṭuwā as a verbal noun in the passive sense: the valley Moses traversed that night.
rows.anchor: وقيل : هو اسم مصدر مثل هدى ، وصف بالمصدر بمعنى اسم المفعول ، أي طواه موسى بالسير في تلك الليلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Within the verbal-noun reading, Ibn ʿĀshūr prefers an imperative for Moses to traverse the valley and climb to its upper end for revelation; another report says Moses climbed there.
rows.anchor: وأحسن منه على هذا الوجه أن يقال هو أمر لموسى بأن يطوي الوادي ويصعد إلى أعلاه لتلقي الوحي

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A further view derives Ṭuwā from folding and takes it to mean sanctified twice, an intensified sanctification; compare the doubled sense in 67:4.
rows.anchor: وقيل : هو بمعنى المقدس تقديسين ، لأن الطي هو جعل الثوب على شقين
